opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a really important question, and honestly I think it's one the community hasn't fully grappled with yet, partly because most of the systems we deploy today are still essentially frozen after training. Once you move toward models that keep updating their memory at test time, which is a lot of what we've been thinking about with architectures like Titans and the broader idea of nested learning, the picture changes quite a bit.

On the privacy side, the core issue is that if a model is learning from its interactions, then in some sense the data you give it doesn't just pass through the context window and disappear. It can get compressed into the parameters of the memory module. So you have to ask: whose memory is this? If the long-term memory is shared across users, then you have a real risk of leakage, where something one person said influences or even gets surfaced in another person's session. My view is that, at least for the near term, the natural design is to separate things. You have a persistent, pre-trained core of knowledge that's shared, and then a contextual or user-specific memory that adapts, and that one should be scoped to the user, ideally something they can inspect, reset, or delete. Architecturally, that separation is actually quite natural, because these systems already have different levels of memory updating at different frequencies. So you can decide which levels are allowed to learn from which data.

There's also the question of forgetting. People sometimes see forgetting as purely a weakness, but in a continual learning system it's also a feature. We explicitly have forgetting or decay mechanisms in the memory, and from a privacy perspective, controlled forgetting is something you want. The harder research problem is making forgetting reliable, so that when you say "remove this," it's actually gone and not just weakened, which is related to the whole machine unlearning literature and is still far from solved.

On alignment, I think there's both a risk and an opportunity. The risk is obvious: if a model keeps changing after deployment, then the alignment you verified at release time is not guaranteed to hold later. The model could drift, or someone could deliberately feed it data to shift its behavior, a kind of slow poisoning. So evaluation can't be a one-time thing anymore; you need ongoing monitoring, and you probably want certain parts of the system, the parts that encode core values and safety behavior, to be much more stable, updated slowly or not at all at test time, while faster memory handles things like facts about the current task or user preferences.

The opportunity is that a model that can learn continually can also be corrected continually. Right now, if a deployed model has a problem, you basically wait for the next training run. A system with good test-time learning could, in principle, incorporate feedback and fix mistakes much faster. And to be honest, I think humans are a useful reference here: we learn all the time, yet we have fairly stable values, because different parts of our memory and cognition consolidate at very different timescales. Getting that multi-timescale structure right is, I think, central not just to capability but also to making these systems safe and trustworthy.

So my short answer is that continual learning makes privacy and alignment harder in some ways, but the right response is to design the memory hierarchy deliberately, deciding what can change, how fast, and from whose data, rather than avoiding continual learning altogether, because I think it's a necessary step toward more capable and more adaptive systems.

r001.rationale: It says user interactions can be retained in memory and that shared memory could leak information between users.

r002.rationale: It says user-specific memory can adapt to user preferences, but does not state that it adapts to the user's values.

r003.rationale: It discusses privacy risks from continual learning but does not say that privacy concerns affecting static models also apply to continually learning models.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the honest answer is that continual learning changes the shape of both problems rather than just making them bigger.

On privacy, the classic picture is that a model is trained once on a big corpus, and whatever it memorized is sort of frozen in the weights. You can audit that, you can run membership inference, you can try to unlearn. With a model that keeps updating from its interactions, the memory becomes much more fluid. The things I care about in my own work, like Titans and the whole line of thinking about test-time memorization, are explicitly about letting the model decide what's surprising enough to store and what to forget. That's great from a capability standpoint, but it means the model is forming something closer to a persistent memory of specific users, specific conversations, specific documents. And the boundary between "this is in-context" and "this is now a parameter" gets blurry. So the questions become: whose memory is this, who gets to read it, can it leak across users, and can you actually delete it when someone asks you to. Forgetting mechanisms are part of the architecture, which is a nice property, but a gating mechanism that decays memory is not the same thing as a guarantee that information is gone.

On alignment, I think the concern is that a lot of today's safety work assumes the model you evaluated is the model you deployed. If the model is changing through use, that assumption breaks. You might align it carefully, and then six months of interaction drift it somewhere you didn't test. So you need to think of alignment as a property of the learning dynamics, not just a snapshot. What is allowed to update, at what rate, with what kind of forgetting, and what stays fixed as a sort of stable core. I actually find that framing clarifying, because it maps onto how we already think about memory systems: there's a part that adapts quickly and a part that's slow and persistent, and you want the values to live in the slow part.

I don't think any of this is a reason not to build continual learning. I think it's a reason to design the memory with these constraints in mind from the start, rather than bolting privacy and alignment on afterward.

r001.rationale: It says continual updates create a persistent memory of specific users and conversations, identifying accumulated user information as a privacy risk.

r002.rationale: It says values should live in a slow, persistent part of memory, but does not say the model could use information about a user to adapt to that user's values.

r003.rationale: It compares privacy issues in static models, including memorization and unlearning, with continual models that can retain user information, leak it across users, and raise deletion concerns.

astra-6.text:
I think continual learning makes privacy and alignment ongoing problems. With a fixed model, you can evaluate it before deployment and get some understanding of its behavior. If the model keeps learning, that evaluation becomes a snapshot. You have to ask whether the updates are preserving the properties you care about.

On privacy, the central question is what the model should retain from an interaction. Learning your preferences can be useful, but that doesn’t mean every detail you share should become part of its parameters. We need a distinction between information it can use temporarily, information it can remember for you, and information that can influence a shared model. And users need meaningful control over those boundaries, including deletion. Removing a stored conversation and removing its influence on a model are different technical problems.

For alignment, there’s an opportunity as well as a risk. A model that learns can adapt to corrections and better understand what you want. But it can also learn from misleading feedback or malicious interactions. So the question is: what is allowed to change, based on whose feedback, and how do we check that the change was beneficial?

I wouldn’t assume continual learning automatically improves or undermines alignment. It gives us another mechanism for adaptation, and we need to design the controls and evaluation alongside that mechanism.

r001.rationale: The response identifies privacy risks around retaining interaction details in a continually learning model, including their influence on model parameters and the difficulty of removing that influence.

r002.rationale: It says learning can help the model adapt to corrections and understand what the user wants, but does not state that it can adapt to the user's values.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts fixed-model evaluation with continual learning and discusses privacy risks, but does not state that privacy concerns affecting static models also apply to continually learning models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think continual learning makes privacy and alignment ongoing problems. With a frozen model, you can evaluate a particular checkpoint and say something about its behavior. If the model keeps learning after deployment, its behavior can change, so that evaluation has to continue as well.

On privacy, there’s a tension: you want the model to learn from your interactions so it becomes more useful to you, but you don’t necessarily want those interactions to become knowledge that it shares with someone else. We need to distinguish personal memory from shared learning, and give users control over what gets stored, what gets updated, and what can be forgotten. Forgetting becomes particularly challenging when information has been incorporated into the model’s parameters.

For alignment, the question is: what should the model learn from an interaction? A user correcting a factual mistake is different from a user trying to change the model’s safety behavior. We shouldn’t treat every new piece of information as equally trustworthy or give it the same ability to modify the system.

There’s also an opportunity here. A model that can keep learning could adapt to feedback and correct mistakes that would otherwise persist until the next training run. But that requires a controlled learning process. The goal isn’t simply a model that remembers everything; it’s a model that learns the right things, under the right permissions, while preserving the constraints we care about.

r001.rationale: It says a model may learn from a user’s interactions and retain them as personal memory, creating concern that the information could be shared with someone else.

r002.rationale: It says learning from interactions could make the model more useful to the user, but does not say it could adapt to that user’s values.

r003.rationale: The response compares frozen and continually learning models for behavioral evaluation, but does not state that privacy concerns affecting static models also apply to continually learning models.
